`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
`piton compile` gives:

```ts
import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
import spec from '../spec/app.pi';

const button = SaveButton;
const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
```

It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.

## 15. Working on a specbase

1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
   follow them only when relevant.
3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
     `lib/` folder;
   - lowerCamelCase property names;
   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
5. **Validate.**
   - Run `piton check`.
   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
   - Run `piton format --check`.
6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in

# Ribbon Scope

## How To Build

A RibbonScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The ribbon along the top of the main window: tabs, each holding the application's commands for one area of work in labelled groups.

### Shape

#### Description

A ribbon runs along the top of the window, in the colours of the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope), a row of tabs, 32 pixels tall, above the command area. The tabs are flat: each is only its label, with 8 pixels either side of it, and no borders, no rounded corners, and no line anywhere, neither between the tabs nor between the tab row and the commands. The tab row has a background of its own, a step lighter than the command area, #333333 in dark mode; a closed tab has no background, and an open tab takes the command area's background, #222222 in dark mode, so it and the commands beneath it read as one piece, the edge of the colour the only edge. In light mode the same steps run the other way, the tab row a step darker than the command area. Opening and closing tabs never shifts a label.
A tab whose commands work on one of the chat input's modes, as the Code and Spec tabs do, takes that mode's colour: its label is in the mode's colour while the tab is closed, and while open, the tab is tinted with it instead and its label is the tab's own colour. Each such tab says more. Its tabs are, in order: Project, Code, Spec, Research, and Application. The window always opens on Project. Beneath the tabs, the selected tab's commands sit in groups. There is no raw output view and no toggle for one.

#### Keyboard

<Alt+1> opens the first tab, <Alt+2> the second, and so on, through each tab in the order the tabs are shown, <Alt+5> opening Application. Each opens its tab alone, as clicking it does, and expands the ribbon first if it is collapsed. A number past the last tab does nothing. Like the ribbon's other shortcuts, they do nothing while an inset panel is open. A tab's tooltip doesn't give its shortcut, since a tab has no tooltip.

#### Opening Several Tabs

Clicking a tab opens it alone, as usual. Ctrl+clicking one (Cmd+click on macOS) opens it alongside whichever tabs are already open, or, if it is already open, closes it, so any number of tabs can be open at once. The last open tab can't be closed this way: Ctrl+clicking it leaves it open. Every open tab shows as selected.
The command area then holds the groups of every open tab side by side, in the order of the tabs rather than the order they were opened, with the same divider between one tab's groups and the next as between any groups. An open tab with no commands adds nothing, and "No commands yet" shows only when none of the open tabs has any. When the groups are wider than the window, the command area scrolls sideways. The command area stays the same height however many tabs are open.
Double-clicking a tab still collapses the ribbon, and expanding it again shows the same tabs open. Which tabs are open isn't kept between

##### Launches

the window always opens with only Project open.

#### Left Container

At the left end of the bar, left of the tab bar itself rather than inside it, so the tab bar's own padding and bottom line don't reach it, sits the left container. It holds, in order, the project indicator, the collapse chevron, and the activity spinner, and can hold other things after them. It is the same whether the ribbon is expanded, beside the tabs, or collapsed, leading the row of primary commands.
It runs from the top of the bar down to the line along its bottom, never over it, so it is the same height expanded and collapsed. Everything in it is vertically centred in that height, with no gap between one thing and the next and no padding around them: each thing's own size is all the room it takes. The container shrinks to fit what it holds, and when it holds nothing, it isn't there at all.

#### Right Container

At the right end of the bar, right of the tabs, or of the primary commands when the ribbon is collapsed, sits the right container. It holds nothing yet, and can hold other things. It lays out what it holds as the left container does: vertically centred, with no gap between things and no padding around them, shrinking to fit, and not there at all while it holds nothing, as it is now.

#### Activity

The indicator and list of the [RunningActivityScope](../../../scope/running-activity/index.md#running-activity-scope) sit in the left container, just right of the collapse chevron. While nothing is running, the spinner isn't there, and the left container shrinks around the project indicator and the chevron.

#### Project Indicator

The [ProjectIndicator](../project-indicator/index.md#project-indicator) leads the left container, a solid block the full height of the bar down to the line along its bottom, ending on that line. It is the same height, and what it shows is in the same place, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed. There is no divider between it and what

##### Follows

the change of background is the edge. The collapse chevron

sits just after it, and the activity spinner just after the chevron.

#### Groups

Groups have no titles shown. They sit side by side, and between one group and the next, 4 pixels from the buttons either side, stands a

##### Divider

a bar 4 pixels wide, in the tab row's background colour, as

tall as the buttons, from the top of the first to the bottom of the last, with its ends softly rounded. The first group starts 8 pixels from the command area's left edge. Each group still has a name, saying what its commands have in common, which is the divider's tooltip and what assistive technology reads for it.
A tab with no commands reads "No commands yet".

#### Tabs

Each tab is a scope of its own, which says what groups and commands it holds, and what each command does.

##### Project

[RibbonProjectTabScope](./project-tab/index.md#ribbon-project-tab-scope)

##### Code

[RibbonCodeTabScope](./code-tab/index.md#ribbon-code-tab-scope)

##### Spec

[RibbonSpecTabScope](./spec-tab/index.md#ribbon-spec-tab-scope)

##### Research

[RibbonResearchTabScope](./research-tab/index.md#ribbon-research-tab-scope)

##### Application

[RibbonApplicationTabScope](./application-tab/index.md#ribbon-application-tab-scope)

#### Commands

A command button is one of two sizes, and each tab says which of its commands are which:

- full: its small icon above its label, centred, exactly two slim buttons stacked tall
- slim: 27 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label
- small: only in the collapsed ribbon: 22 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label, and only as wide as they are

Buttons side by side are 4 pixels apart. Slim buttons side by side stack down instead, top aligned, two to a column, 4 pixels apart, each column as wide as its widest button and each button as wide as its column; a third starts the next column, 4 pixels along. A button's label is in the regular text colour, its icon beside or above it in the same colour, with 8 pixels either side of them. A full button always stands alone. A slim button fills only its column's width: nowhere does a button stretch to fill a row.
Every command starts from the top of its group, so the commands of a tab all start at the same line. A full button is always two slim buttons stacked tall, never shorter or taller, however much its icon and label would take, alone or beside any column.
Every button is square, with no rounded corners, and no border. Its background is clearly apart from the commands' area behind it, though still quiet: #444444 on the #222222 area in dark mode, white laid about an eighth of the way over the area, and not quite half way in light mode, rather than a colour of its own, so it stays as far apart from a tinted body too, lighter in both modes, and more so while hovered; while pressed it darkens instead. An on or off setting, like dark mode, is a switch rather than a button, and has no background of its own: the switch and its label sit straight on the commands' area, with nothing behind them, as wide as a button of its size and as tall as the switch and its label need.
A command's tooltip explains what it does rather than repeating its label, and gives its keyboard shortcut if it has one.
A command can be marked primary; each tab says which of its commands are.
A command that can't run is disabled, not hidden, and its tooltip says why.

#### Height

The commands drive the height: the command area is as tall as the tallest column of the open tabs, padded 8 pixels above and below, and nothing more. Since no column holds more than two slim buttons, and a full button is two slim buttons tall, the tallest the command area gets is two slim buttons with 4 pixels between them, padded: 74 pixels, and never more. A tab whose tallest column is two slim buttons, or that has a full button, is taller than one of a single slim button, and a tab with no commands, which is only its "No commands yet" padded the same way, is the shortest of all. So switching tabs can change the command area's height, and the window beneath moves with it.
There are 8 pixels of padding at either end, and "No commands yet" keeps 8 pixels from the left edge too.

#### Collapsing

The ribbon collapses, and expands again, with a chevron button in the left container, after the project indicator, by double-clicking a tab, or with Ctrl+F1 (Cmd+F1 on macOS). Whether it is collapsed is one of the [UserPreferencesScope](../../../scope/user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope).
The chevron button is square, 22 pixels on each side, its icon centred in it. It is the same size, and its icon the same size, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed: only the way the chevron points changes.
Collapsed, the tabs go away too. The ribbon becomes a single thin row, exactly as tall as the row of tabs is when expanded, its bottom line where the tab row's is, so collapsing or expanding moves nothing above that line, led by the left container, the same as beside the tabs, the project indicator filling the row's height, and then every primary command, from all of the tabs, as small buttons: a small icon beside its label, and dark mode as a small switch with no background, only as wide as it and its label. Every one is only as wide as its own icon and label, 8 pixels from the next, whatever the tab it comes from calls it; a command that is slim in its tab doesn't grow to fill the row. They keep the order of their tabs, with a thin vertical divider between the commands of one tab and the next, and keep their tooltips and disabled states. The right container, when it holds anything, ends the row. Every control in the row, the dividers and the containers' contents included, is vertically centred in it.
When the commands and dividers are wider than the room between the left container and the right container, or the right end of the row, that stretch of the row scrolls sideways, as the expanded command area does. The containers stay where they are, never scrolled away or squeezed, and nothing in the row shrinks to fit.

# Ribbon Scope

## How To Build

A RibbonScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The ribbon along the top of the main window: tabs, each holding the application's commands for one area of work in labelled groups.

### Shape

#### Description

A ribbon runs along the top of the window, in the colours of the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope), a row of tabs, 32 pixels tall, above the command area. The tabs are flat: each is only its label, with 8 pixels either side of it, and no borders, no rounded corners, and no line anywhere, neither between the tabs nor between the tab row and the commands. The tab row has a background of its own, a step lighter than the command area, #333333 in dark mode; a closed tab has no background, and an open tab takes the command area's background, #222222 in dark mode, so it and the commands beneath it read as one piece, the edge of the colour the only edge. In light mode the same steps run the other way, the tab row a step darker than the command area. Opening and closing tabs never shifts a label.
A tab whose commands work on one of the chat input's modes, as the Code and Spec tabs do, takes that mode's colour: its label is in the mode's colour while the tab is closed, and while open, the tab is tinted with it instead and its label is the tab's own colour. Each such tab says more. Its tabs are, in order: Project, Code, Spec, Research, and Application. The window always opens on Project. Beneath the tabs, the selected tab's commands sit in groups. There is no raw output view and no toggle for one.

#### Keyboard

<Alt+1> opens the first tab, <Alt+2> the second, and so on, through each tab in the order the tabs are shown, <Alt+5> opening Application. Each opens its tab alone, as clicking it does, and expands the ribbon first if it is collapsed. A number past the last tab does nothing. Like the ribbon's other shortcuts, they do nothing while an inset panel is open. A tab's tooltip doesn't give its shortcut, since a tab has no tooltip.

#### Opening Several Tabs

Clicking a tab opens it alone, as usual. Ctrl+clicking one (Cmd+click on macOS) opens it alongside whichever tabs are already open, or, if it is already open, closes it, so any number of tabs can be open at once. The last open tab can't be closed this way: Ctrl+clicking it leaves it open. Every open tab shows as selected.
The command area then holds the groups of every open tab side by side, in the order of the tabs rather than the order they were opened, with the same divider between one tab's groups and the next as between any groups. An open tab with no commands adds nothing, and "No commands yet" shows only when none of the open tabs has any. When the groups are wider than the window, the command area scrolls sideways. The command area stays the same height however many tabs are open.
Double-clicking a tab still collapses the ribbon, and expanding it again shows the same tabs open. Which tabs are open isn't kept between

##### Launches

the window always opens with only Project open.

#### Left Container

At the left end of the bar, left of the tab bar itself rather than inside it, so the tab bar's own padding and bottom line don't reach it, sits the left container. It holds, in order, the project indicator, the collapse chevron, and the activity spinner, and can hold other things after them. It is the same whether the ribbon is expanded, beside the tabs, or collapsed, leading the row of primary commands.
It runs from the top of the bar down to the line along its bottom, never over it, so it is the same height expanded and collapsed. Everything in it is vertically centred in that height, with no gap between one thing and the next and no padding around them: each thing's own size is all the room it takes. The container shrinks to fit what it holds, and when it holds nothing, it isn't there at all.

#### Right Container

At the right end of the bar, right of the tabs, or of the primary commands when the ribbon is collapsed, sits the right container. It holds nothing yet, and can hold other things. It lays out what it holds as the left container does: vertically centred, with no gap between things and no padding around them, shrinking to fit, and not there at all while it holds nothing, as it is now.

#### Activity

The indicator and list of the [RunningActivityScope](../../../scope/running-activity/index.md#running-activity-scope) sit in the left container, just right of the collapse chevron. While nothing is running, the spinner isn't there, and the left container shrinks around the project indicator and the chevron.

#### Project Indicator

The [ProjectIndicator](../project-indicator/index.md#project-indicator) leads the left container, a solid block the full height of the bar down to the line along its bottom, ending on that line. It is the same height, and what it shows is in the same place, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed. There is no divider between it and what

##### Follows

the change of background is the edge. The collapse chevron

sits just after it, and the activity spinner just after the chevron.

#### Groups

Groups have no titles shown. They sit side by side, and between one group and the next, 4 pixels from the buttons either side, stands a

##### Divider

a bar 4 pixels wide, in the tab row's background colour, as

tall as the buttons, from the top of the first to the bottom of the last, with its ends softly rounded. The first group starts 8 pixels from the command area's left edge. Each group still has a name, saying what its commands have in common, which is the divider's tooltip and what assistive technology reads for it.
A tab with no commands reads "No commands yet".

#### Tabs

Each tab is a scope of its own, which says what groups and commands it holds, and what each command does.

##### Project

[RibbonProjectTabScope](./project-tab/index.md#ribbon-project-tab-scope)

##### Code

[RibbonCodeTabScope](./code-tab/index.md#ribbon-code-tab-scope)

##### Spec

[RibbonSpecTabScope](./spec-tab/index.md#ribbon-spec-tab-scope)

##### Research

[RibbonResearchTabScope](./research-tab/index.md#ribbon-research-tab-scope)

##### Application

[RibbonApplicationTabScope](./application-tab/index.md#ribbon-application-tab-scope)

#### Commands

A command button is one of two sizes, and each tab says which of its commands are which:

- full: its small icon above its label, centred, exactly two slim buttons stacked tall
- slim: 27 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label
- small: only in the collapsed ribbon: 22 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label, and only as wide as they are

Buttons side by side are 4 pixels apart. Slim buttons side by side stack down instead, top aligned, two to a column, 4 pixels apart, each column as wide as its widest button and each button as wide as its column; a third starts the next column, 4 pixels along. A button's label is in the regular text colour, its icon beside or above it in the same colour, with 8 pixels either side of them. A full button always stands alone. A slim button fills only its column's width: nowhere does a button stretch to fill a row.
Every command starts from the top of its group, so the commands of a tab all start at the same line. A full button is always two slim buttons stacked tall, never shorter or taller, however much its icon and label would take, alone or beside any column.
Every button is square, with no rounded corners, and no border. Its background is clearly apart from the commands' area behind it, though still quiet: #444444 on the #222222 area in dark mode, white laid about an eighth of the way over the area, and not quite half way in light mode, rather than a colour of its own, so it stays as far apart from a tinted body too, lighter in both modes, and more so while hovered; while pressed it darkens instead. An on or off setting, like dark mode, is a switch rather than a button, and has no background of its own: the switch and its label sit straight on the commands' area, with nothing behind them, as wide as a button of its size and as tall as the switch and its label need.
A command's tooltip explains what it does rather than repeating its label, and gives its keyboard shortcut if it has one.
A command can be marked primary; each tab says which of its commands are.
A command that can't run is disabled, not hidden, and its tooltip says why.

#### Height

The commands drive the height: the command area is as tall as the tallest column of the open tabs, padded 8 pixels above and below, and nothing more. Since no column holds more than two slim buttons, and a full button is two slim buttons tall, the tallest the command area gets is two slim buttons with 4 pixels between them, padded: 74 pixels, and never more. A tab whose tallest column is two slim buttons, or that has a full button, is taller than one of a single slim button, and a tab with no commands, which is only its "No commands yet" padded the same way, is the shortest of all. So switching tabs can change the command area's height, and the window beneath moves with it.
There are 8 pixels of padding at either end, and "No commands yet" keeps 8 pixels from the left edge too.

#### Collapsing

The ribbon collapses, and expands again, with a chevron button in the left container, after the project indicator, by double-clicking a tab, or with Ctrl+F1 (Cmd+F1 on macOS). Whether it is collapsed is one of the [UserPreferencesScope](../../../scope/user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope).
The chevron button is square, 22 pixels on each side, its icon centred in it. It is the same size, and its icon the same size, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed: only the way the chevron points changes.
Collapsed, the tabs go away too. The ribbon becomes a single thin row, exactly as tall as the row of tabs is when expanded, its bottom line where the tab row's is, so collapsing or expanding moves nothing above that line, led by the left container, the same as beside the tabs, the project indicator filling the row's height, and then every primary command, from all of the tabs, as small buttons: a small icon beside its label, and dark mode as a small switch with no background, only as wide as it and its label. Every one is only as wide as its own icon and label, 8 pixels from the next, whatever the tab it comes from calls it; a command that is slim in its tab doesn't grow to fill the row. They keep the order of their tabs, with a thin vertical divider between the commands of one tab and the next, and keep their tooltips and disabled states. The right container, when it holds anything, ends the row. Every control in the row, the dividers and the containers' contents included, is vertically centred in it.
When the commands and dividers are wider than the room between the left container and the right container, or the right end of the row, that stretch of the row scrolls sideways, as the expanded command area does. The containers stay where they are, never scrolled away or squeezed, and nothing in the row shrinks to fit.

# Ribbon Application Tab Scope

## How To Build

A RibbonApplicationTabScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonApplicationTabScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The ribbon's Application tab: the commands for the application itself, rather than the project.

### Shape

#### Description

The Application tab of the ribbon, last of the tabs.

#### Groups

```
appearance: An "Appearance" group holds the Dark mode command, then the Brightness command beneath it.
preferences: A "Preferences" group holds the Settings command.
```

#### Commands

```
darkMode: A "Dark mode" switch, on while the window is in dark mode. Switching it changes the window between light and dark mode straight away, and saves the choice among the [UserPreferencesScope](../../../../scope/user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope). A choice that can't be saved shows a notification titled "Could not save dark mode", with why.
  It is primary, and slim: the switch takes the room of a slim button, with no background of its own.
brightness: A "Brightness" slider, beneath Dark mode in the same column: a sun icon, then a horizontal slider 120 pixels wide, then the setting as a signed number, muted, "0" at the middle. Like the switch, it has no background of its own, and sits straight on the commands' area, as tall as a slim button. Its tooltip says it makes the whole interface lighter or darker while keeping its contrast, and that double-clicking it resets it.
  Dragging it changes the brightness of the interface, as the [ThemeScope](../../../theme/index.md#theme-scope) says, straight away as it moves, and saves it among the [UserPreferencesScope](../../../../scope/user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) once it is let go. Double-clicking it puts it back to 0. Its range is whatever the theme allows in the current mode, and each mode keeps its own setting, so switching modes moves the slider to that mode's. It is not primary, so the collapsed ribbon doesn't show it.
settings: A "Settings" button with a gear icon. Clicking it opens the [SettingsWindowScope](../../../../scope/settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope), where the system prompt each chat tab sends is edited. Its tooltip says so, and gives its keyboard shortcut, Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS).
  It is primary, and a full button.
```
